subject: math
title: Grade 1 Equal and Not Equal
seo_title: Grade 1 Equal and Not Equal Worksheets (= and ≠): Free Math with Answer Key (BC Curriculum)
meta_desc: Free Grade 1 math worksheets on equal and not equal for the BC curriculum: balances, equal groups, the = and ≠ signs, is 4 + 3 the same as 5 + 2, more, fewer or the same, and making both sides equal. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: The = sign means “is the same as.” The ≠ sign means “is not equal to.”
key_sub: 4 + 3 = 5 + 2 because both sides are 7. 4 + 4 ≠ 5 + 2 because 8 is not 7. In 6 + 2 = □ + 3, the box is 5, not 8.
body_html:
= means “the same as”

The = sign means is the same as. Both sides must have the same amount. It does not mean “the answer comes next.” Think of a balance. When both sides are the same, it is level.

≠ means “is not equal to”

When the two sides are not the same, use ≠. The side with more goes down.

Two sidesLeftRightSign
4 + 3 and 5 + 277=
4 + 4 and 5 + 287≠
9 − 2 and 4 + 377=
10 + 6 and 8 + 81616=

Count. Do not just look.

A longer row does not always have more. Count each group. If the numbers are the same, the groups are equal.

More, fewer or the same

Line the groups up. The extra ones show how many more.

Example

Noah has 9 cubes. Sofia has 6. How many more does Noah have?

Count up from 6 to 9: 7, 8, 9. That is 3.

Answer: 3 more

Make both sides equal

A box □ is a number you do not know. Find the side you know first. Then make the other side the same.

Example

6 + 2 = □ + 3

The left side is 6 + 2 = 8. Now □ + 3 = 8. Count up from 3: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. That is 5.

Answer: 5

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
6 + 2 = □ + 3, so □ = 88 is the left side. □ + 3 = 8, so □ = 5
6 + 2 = □ + 3, so □ = 11 (adding all)Make both sides the same. Do not add everything
The longer row has moreCount each row. Spread-out dots are not more
4 + 3 and 5 + 2 are not equal because the numbers are differentFind each side: both are 7, so they are equal
7 = 8 − 1 is wrong because the answer is firstThe = sign can come first. Both sides are 7

faq.q: What does equality and inequality mean in Grade 1 math in BC?
faq.a: It means knowing when two amounts are the same (equal) and when they are not (not equal). In the BC Grade 1 Patterning standard, students use balances and objects to show that 4 + 3 = 5 + 2 and that 4 + 4 ≠ 5 + 2.

faq.q: How do you teach the equal sign in Grade 1?
faq.a: Use a pan balance: when both sides have the same amount, it is level. This shows that = means “is the same as,” not “the answer comes next,” so 3 + 4 = 5 + 2 is true.

faq.q: What does the not equal sign (≠) mean?
faq.a: The ≠ sign means “is not equal to.” For example, 8 ≠ 7 and 5 + 3 ≠ 7, because 8 is not the same as 7.
Find the side you know first: 6 + 2 = 8. Then ask what number plus 3 makes 8. Count up from 3 to 8, so the box is 5, not 8.

sets.title: Make both sides equal: word problems

items.q: Kai sees 5 orcas. Then 2 more swim by. Mei sees 7 orcas. Do they see the same number?
items.e: Kai: 5 + 2 = 7. Mei: 7. Both are 7, so yes: 5 + 2 = 7.

items.q: Simran has 8 stickers. She gets 3 more. Owen has 10. Do they have the same number?
items.e: Simran: 8 + 3 = 11. Owen: 10. 11 is not 10, so no: 8 + 3 ≠ 10.

items.q: In Stanley Park, 6 kids hike. 4 more join. 5 kids bike. 5 more join. Are the same number of kids hiking and biking?
items.e: Hike: 6 + 4 = 10. Bike: 5 + 5 = 10. Both are 10, so yes: 6 + 4 = 5 + 5.

items.q: Noah has 12 cedar cones. He gives 4 away. Chloe has 10. She gives 2 away. Do they have the same number now?
items.e: Noah: 12 − 4 = 8. Chloe: 10 − 2 = 8. Both have 8, so yes: 12 − 4 = 10 − 2.

items.q: Ava has 6 apples and 2 pears. Lucas has 3 apples. How many pears must he get to have the same?
items.e: Ava has 6 + 2 = 8. Lucas needs 8 too. 3 + □ = 8. Count up from 3 to 8: 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. That is 5. So he needs 5 pears. Not 8: that is Ava’s total.

items.q: Jasleen has 4 red crayons and 5 blue crayons. Ryan has 9 crayons. Which number sentence fits?
items.e: Jasleen has 4 + 5. Ryan has 9. 4 + 5 = 9, so they are the same: 4 + 5 = 9.

items.q: Zara has a pack of 10 stickers and 5 more. Harjot has 15. Do they have the same number?
items.e: Zara: 10 + 5 = 15. Harjot: 15. Both have 15, so yes. Not 6: the pack is 10, not 1.

items.q: Leah has 14 hockey cards. Wei has 10. How many more does Wei need to have the same?
items.e: Leah has 14. Wei has 10. 10 + 4 = 14, so Wei needs 4 cards. Not 14: that is how many Leah has.

items.q: At the Terry Fox Run, Room 1 has 6 girls and 4 boys. Room 2 has 3 girls and some boys. Both rooms have the same number. How many boys are in Room 2?
items.e: Room 1: 6 + 4 = 10. Room 2 must have 10 too. 3 + □ = 10. 3 + 7 = 10, so 7 boys. Not 10: that is all of Room 1.

items.q: The class needs 20 apples for a field trip. Olivia brings 12. Arjun brings 6. Is that 20 apples?
items.e: 12 + 6 = 18. 18 is not 20, so no: 12 + 6 ≠ 20. They need 2 more.

items.q: A tower has 7 blue blocks and 5 red blocks. Another has 10 green blocks. How many green blocks must you add to make them the same?
items.e: 7 + 5 = 12. 10 + □ = 12. 10 + 2 = 12, so add 2 blocks. Not 12: that is the first tower.

items.q: Team A has 9 kids. 6 more come. Team B has 10 kids. How many more kids must come to Team B to make it the same?
items.e: Team A: 9 + 6 = 15. Team B: 10 + □ = 15. 10 + 5 = 15, so 5 kids. Not 15: that is all of Team A.

items.q: Ethan has 8 cards. He gives 3 away. Sofia has 2 cards. She gets 3 more. They have the same. Which number sentence fits?
At the lake, Canoe A has 5 kids and 4 adults. Canoe B has 6 kids and some adults. Both canoes have the same number of people. How many adults are in Canoe B?
items.e: Canoe A: 5 + 4 = 9. Canoe B: 6 + □ = 9. 6 + 3 = 9, so 3 adults. Not 9: that is everyone in Canoe A.

items.q: On BC Ferries, Liam counts 7 red cars and 5 blue cars. Hana counts 12 cars. Which number sentence fits?
items.e: Liam counts 7 + 5 = 12. Hana counts 12. They are the same: 7 + 5 = 12.

items.q: 8 people get on a SkyTrain car. Then 6 more get on. Car 2 has 14 people. Do the cars have the same number?
items.e: Car 1: 8 + 6 = 14. Car 2: 14. Both have 14, so yes: 8 + 6 = 14.

items.q: Mateo has 13 blocks in a tower. Sofia has 9. How many must Mateo take off to make them the same?
items.e: Mateo has 13. Sofia has 9. 9 + 4 = 13, so Mateo takes off 4 blocks. 13 − 4 = 9. Not 13: then he has 0 left.

items.q: Kai has 9 shells. Emma has 5. Kai gives Emma some. Now they have the same. How many did Kai give?
items.e: Together they have 9 + 5 = 14. The same is 7 each. Kai gives 2: 9 − 2 = 7 and 5 + 2 = 7. So 2 shells. Not 4: then Kai has 5 and Emma has 9.

items.q: Lucas has 6 red and 6 green marbles. Ava has 10 blue and 2 yellow marbles. Which number sentence fits?
At Whistler, 8 kids ski and 3 kids snowboard. In a second group, 5 kids ski. How many must snowboard to make the groups the same?
items.e: Group 1: 8 + 3 = 11. Group 2: 5 + □ = 11. 5 + 6 = 11, so 6 kids. Not 11: that is all of Group 1.
